title: YOUR MARRIAGE WAS NEVER ONLY ABOUT THE TWO OF YOU
paragraphs:
YOUR MARRIAGE WAS NEVER ONLY ABOUT THE TWO OF YOU
How Marriage Points to Christ and the Church—and Why the Gospel Can Rewrite What Sin, Betrayal, Exhaustion, and Broken Expectations Have Tried to Destroy
There is something almost frightening about the way the Bible talks about marriage.
Because Scripture refuses to let marriage remain merely romantic.

It will not allow us to reduce it to chemistry, compatibility, wedding photographs, anniversaries, children, shared bills, physical intimacy, or two people trying their best to stay together until death.
Then somehow, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he sees something infinitely larger standing behind them.
Then he writes words that should make every married Christian—and every Christian who hopes to marry someday—stop for a moment:
And then Paul reveals what he has been talking about:
“…ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.”
“…but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the church.”
Paul has just quoted Genesis 2:24—“the two shall become one flesh”—and then tells us that this ancient mystery reaches beyond Adam and Eve.
It points to a Bridegroom who refuses to abandon the Bride He purchased with His own blood.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely, “Is my spouse making me happy?”
A much more uncomfortable question enters the room:
What is my marriage saying about Jesus?
Especially when the marriage is hurting.
Especially when you are reading this beside someone who once felt like home but lately feels like a stranger.
Especially when conversations have become arguments.
Especially when affection has become routine.
Especially when the bedroom has become cold.
Especially when resentment has learned where you sleep.
Especially when both of you know exactly which words will wound the deepest.
Your Facebook pictures still look fine.
You still smile when someone asks how the family is doing.
But God sees the silence in the car after church.
God sees the messages you deleted.
God sees the bitterness you rehearse while your spouse sleeps.
God sees the apology you refuse to give.
God sees the loneliness you are embarrassed to admit.
God sees the temptation you have been feeding because you keep telling yourself, “My spouse doesn't understand me anymore.”
And strangely enough, that should not only terrify us.
Because the God who sees the scandal is also the God who specializes in grace.
Marriage begins in Scripture before human rebellion enters the world.
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’ish ’et-’aviv ve’et-’immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Marriage, biblically understood, is not simply two independent lives sharing an address.
God joins a man and woman in a profound covenantal union.
Jesus Himself later reaches back to this creation text when questioned about marriage:
“Therefore what God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Marriage therefore belongs first to God before it belongs to us.
And this is precisely why Christianity has something far deeper to say about marriage than “find the person who completes you.”
Marriage is a gift, but it cannot bear the weight of being your god.
And perhaps some marriages begin healing when two people finally stop demanding from each other what only Jesus can provide.
No sinful human being can carry that expectation indefinitely.
And once Jesus becomes the center rather than the spouse becoming the center, something changes.
Now marriage can become what it was always meant to be:

Paul's words in Ephesians 5 are sometimes discussed almost entirely in terms of authority and submission, and when ripped away from their larger context they can be distorted into something Scripture never intended.
The passage begins its household discussion within a life characterized by being filled with the Spirit, thanksgiving, worship, and mutual Christian humility.
Then Paul tells wives to relate to their husbands in a way that points toward the Church's relationship with Christ.
But husbands are given a command so devastatingly demanding that no Christian man should ever read it casually:
“…καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“…just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Not “I'm the man, so do what I say.”
Not using Bible verses as weapons to protect selfishness.
The Greek verb behind “gave Himself up,” παρέδωκεν — paredōken, carries the sense of handing over or delivering up.
Paul points the husband toward Calvary.
Toward the Son of God laying Himself down for His Bride.
Christian husband, before Ephesians 5 ever becomes a verse you use to examine your wife, it becomes a mirror held in front of you.
Does she encounter something of Christ's sacrificial love through the way you treat her?
When you have the power to humiliate her but choose gentleness instead?
When she needs your attention and your phone is easier?
When saying “I was wrong” feels like dying?
Because sometimes dying to yourself looks remarkably ordinary.
Changing the habit you keep defending.
Praying when you would rather argue.
And wife, the gospel confronts your heart too.
Not with inferiority—Scripture never teaches that women possess less worth before God—but with the call to honor Christ even within the intimate reality of marriage.
The Christian vision is not husband versus wife.
It is husband and wife under Jesus.
Two sinners kneeling beneath the same cross.
Two people who both need mercy.
Two people who both need sanctification.
Two people learning that covenant love becomes most visible not when loving is easy…
And that is where marriage begins preaching.
Because Christ did not love His Church because she was already spotless.
He loved her in order to make her holy.
Ephesians 5 says Christ gave Himself for the Church “that He might sanctify her.”
A husband is not his wife's savior.
But Christian marriage can become a living witness to the kind of covenant faithfulness the Gospel reveals.
The Church's Bridegroom did not wait for His Bride to become beautiful enough to deserve Him.
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned up the addiction.
Not after we finally became religious enough.
This does not mean sin should be ignored.
Grace never means pretending evil is harmless.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical; reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance, safety, and the rebuilding of trust.

And no biblical teaching about marital commitment should ever be twisted into demanding that someone quietly endure violence, coercion, abuse, or serious danger. Seeking safety, pastoral help, professional assistance, and lawful protection where necessary is not a betrayal of Christian faithfulness.
But for many marriages, the enemy is not one spectacular catastrophe.
It is ten thousand tiny withdrawals of love.
One night turning your back instead of reaching across the bed.
One more week without praying together.
One more month living like roommates.
Then one day you look across the room and wonder where the person you married went.
But perhaps they are wondering the same thing about you.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Because Christianity does not say, “Pretend nothing happened.”
Christianity says something far more powerful:
Bring what happened to the cross.
There is no marriage so healthy that it no longer needs grace.
And there is no Christian spouse so mature that repentance has become unnecessary.
Sometimes the most spiritually powerful words spoken in a home are not eloquent prayers.
Because repentance stops asking, “How do I win this argument?”
Imagine what could happen if both spouses began asking that question.
“Jesus, what needs to die in me?”
The obsession with always being right?
Maybe the marriage you keep asking God to change will begin changing when you allow Him to change you.
And perhaps this is one reason marriage points so powerfully toward Christ and His Church.
You can impress people at church.
It is harder to impress someone who has watched you look for your phone while it was already in your hand.
And then comes the terrifying question:
Will you still love me when you know me?
Every human heart asks some version of that question.
And the Gospel answers it at Calvary.
And He loved them all the way to the cross.
Love that confronts sin precisely because it intends redemption.
Love strong enough to tell the truth.
This is why Revelation eventually describes the culmination of redemption with the imagery of a wedding.
“Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come…”
History is moving toward a wedding feast.
The Bible begins with a marriage in Eden.
Near its conclusion, we encounter the marriage supper of the Lamb.
And standing at the center of everything is Jesus Christ—the Bridegroom who purchased His people.
Someone is coming for His Bride.
Every faithful Christian marriage is an imperfect trailer for that coming reality.
We sometimes carry yesterday's pain into today's conversation.
But the picture does not depend upon human perfection.
It depends upon the perfect Christ to whom the picture points.
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply here:
He rewrites the story of the selfish husband who finally falls before God and learns how to serve.
He rewrites the story of the bitter wife whose wounded heart begins surrendering resentment to Christ.
He rewrites the story of the couple who forgot how to talk but begins again with confession.
He rewrites the story of the believer carrying shame from sexual sin who discovers that repentance and Christ's cleansing grace are real.

He rewrites the story of the spouse who thought forgiveness meant pretending nothing happened and learns instead that biblical forgiveness can coexist with truth, wisdom, boundaries, and a serious rebuilding of trust.
And sometimes His rewriting does not look like an instant miracle.
Learning to touch again without fear.
Learning to trust again without pretending.
Learning to pray again after years of spiritual silence.
Sometimes grace looks like two tired people sitting at a kitchen table at midnight saying:
“We cannot keep living like this. Jesus, help us.”
And maybe that is where resurrection begins.
Not when two perfect people finally find each other.
But when two imperfect people discover again that their deepest hope was never each other.
Maybe you are unmarried and wondering whether any of this applies to you.
Because the ultimate marriage pictured in Scripture belongs to every redeemed believer.
Jesus teaches that marriage as we know it does not continue in the resurrection in the same earthly form (Matthew 22:30).
So if you are single, widowed, divorced, abandoned, or never called to marriage, you are not standing outside the greatest love story in Scripture.
If you belong to Christ, you belong to His redeemed people.
Your deepest identity is found in Jesus.
Earthly marriage points toward something greater than itself.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years worshiping the signpost instead of the destination.
“If I could just get married, I would finally be whole.”
“If my spouse would finally change, I would finally have peace.”
But Jesus is quietly confronting that idol.
The One who deserved worship endured mockery.
The hands that fashioned humanity were pierced by humanity.
And He did it to redeem sinners.
You were more sinful than you wanted to admit.
Yet in Christ there is more mercy than you dared to hope.
The Gospel does not tell you to become worthy enough for Jesus.
It tells you that Jesus is worthy.
Maybe your marriage needs that tonight.
Before you send this article to your spouse as ammunition, ask God whether He sent it to you as a mirror.
“Jesus, what are You saying to me?”
What if the thing God wants to rescue first is not your argument…
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, do not hide behind religious language.
Someone quietly considering giving up may need to know that restoration can involve long, difficult faithfulness—and that God is still at work.
Not because every sentence will apply today.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
If this ministry feeds your faith, helps sharpen your walk, or gives you something biblical to place into another person's hands, stay close.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions about Jesus.
And one day every Christian marriage will have finished its temporary assignment.
Every anniversary will have been celebrated for the last time.
Every wedding photograph will belong to another age.
Every ring will have completed its earthly symbolism.
But the reality toward which Christian marriage has been pointing will remain.
The Bride will be with her Bridegroom.
No resentment carried into another morning.
No funeral separating husband from wife.
No sin separating God's people from perfect communion with Him.
So tonight, if you are married, look at the person beside you differently.
They are not merely the person who leaves dishes in the sink.
Not merely the person who forgot the anniversary.
Not merely the person who wounded you.
Not merely the person who disappoints you.
They are a human being made in God's image whom you have been called to love faithfully within covenant.
And your marriage has been given the astonishing privilege of pointing beyond itself.
Maybe your story has chapters you wish had never been written.
Maybe some consequences cannot simply be erased.
But if Christ is present, your worst chapter does not have the authority to name the entire story.
The cross has already proved that God can take the darkest scene imaginable and make it the doorway through which redemption comes.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek help where help is needed.
Rebuild what can faithfully be rebuilt.
And remember why the mystery is so great.
Marriage was never ultimately about proving that two human beings could love each other perfectly.
It was always pointing toward the One who does.
When human love reaches the end of itself, the scarred hands of Jesus still have another page to write.
